```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)     ## to make nice plots
library(glmmTMB)     ## to fit complex mixed effects models
library(lme4)        ## to fit linear and mixed effects models
library(lmerTest)
```

```{r}
soil <- read_csv("data/processed/soil.csv") %>%    ## reads in csv file
  mutate(total = replace_na(total, 0),             ## changes "total" variable
         n_class = replace_na(n_class, 0))         ## changes "n_class" variable
```

# Looking at Land Cover Class Variables

```{r}
# Want to condense the land cover classes to urban vs. green space (which includes open, natural, and agricultural). This is because we just want to compare response variables between urban and non-urban surroundings of gardens.
soil <- soil %>%
    mutate(green250m = open250m + natural250m + ag250m)
```

```{r}
soil %>%
    group_by(site) %>%
    summarize(urban250m = first(urban250m)) %>% 
    ggplot(data = ., aes(x = site, y = urban250m)) + geom_col()
# This makes a bar chart that shows us the percentage of urban land cover surrounding each of the 15 gardens. Forge, MIIS, and Trescony all have 100% urban land cover, while the others indicate that they have some percentage of green space as surrounding land cover.
```

```{r}
# Is there a relationship between percentage of urban land cover and aps count? (looking at total aps count across gardens)
soil %>% 
    group_by(site) %>%
    summarize(garden_apscount = sum(total, na.rm = TRUE),
    urban250m = first(urban250m)) %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x = urban250m, y = garden_apscount)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_abline()
# Made a plot with percentage of urban land cover on the x-axis, and total arthropod count per garden on the y-axis. Added an abline to see any trend. There is one point where the total arthopod count is very high, which seems to be affecting the trend line. Might replot with this garden removed ()

soil %>% 
    group_by(site) %>%
    summarize(garden_apscount = sum(total, na.rm = TRUE),
    urban250m = first(urban250m)) %>% 
    filter(!(site == "Forge")) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = urban250m, y = garden_apscount)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_abline()
# AB line is out of range because of the Forge data but looking at this new plot I can guess that there isn't really a significant trend just from viewing the data plotted out like this.
```

```{r}
# Is there a relationship between percentage of green land cover and aps count? (looking at total aps count across gardens)
soil %>% 
    group_by(site) %>%
    summarize(garden_apscount = sum(total, na.rm = TRUE),
    green250m = first(green250m)) %>% 
    ggplot(aes(x = green250m, y = garden_apscount)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_abline()

# It sort of just seems like the inverse of the relationship between urban land cover and aps count, again we have that outlier with 0 green cover and lots of arthropods. 
```

- Honestly don't think there's really anything significant in land cover class vs. total aps count per garden, at least just looking across sites.

# Is there a relationship between percentage of urban land cover and soil health indicators?

Soil health indicators are ammonium (NH4), nitrate (NO3), and CBH enzyme.

```{r}
# plotting percentage of urban land cover against NH4 measurements
soil %>%
    group_by(site, microhabitat) %>%
    summarize(urban250m = first(urban250m), meanNH4 = mean(nh4_ug_g, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = urban250m, y = meanNH4, color = microhabitat)) + geom_point()
# NH4 in the path microhabitats seem to be generally higher than the measurements in the garden bed, though both microhabitats seem to have a slightly positive relationship between % of urban land cover and mean NH4

# same plot, but looking at NO3
soil %>%
    group_by(site, microhabitat) %>%
    summarize(urban250m = first(urban250m), meanNO3 = mean(no3_ug_g, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = urban250m, y = meanNO3, color = microhabitat)) + geom_point()
# There doesn't seem to be any super strong relationship, perhaps a slight positive correlation

# same plot, but looking at CBH
soil %>%
    group_by(site, microhabitat) %>%
    summarize(urban250m = first(urban250m), meanCBH = mean(cbh_mmol_g_h, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = urban250m, y = meanCBH, color = microhabitat)) + geom_point()
# Same kind of spread, not really any super strong relationship
```

- Just from this quick EDA, there doesn't seem to be a really strong relationship between percentage of urban land cover and any of the soil health indicators.

# Exploring garden characteristic variables

- Specifically, herbspp, numtreeshrub, and veght herbspp: \# of plant species recorded in a sample plot (proxy for plant diversity/richness) numtreeshrub: total \# of tree and shrub individuals in sample plot (proxy for plant abundance) veght: average height (cm) of herbaceous vegetation within a sample plot

```{r}
summary(soil$herbspp)
soil %>%
    group_by(site) %>%
    summarize(herbspp = first(herbspp)) %>%
    head(., 15) %>%
    ggplot(., aes(x = herbspp)) + geom_histogram()
# The histogram shows us that most of the garden meaures of herbspp are clustered on the lower half of the distribution, while a few sit with higher values. So a few gardens might be demonstrating higher plant diversity.


summary(soil$numtreeshrub) # really variable --> it might be that some garden samples had very few plants. Will need to look at the effect of microhabitat as well
soil %>%
    group_by(site) %>%
    summarize(numtreeshrub = first(numtreeshrub)) %>%
    ggplot(., aes(x = numtreeshrub)) + geom_dotplot()
# numtreeshrub seems to be a little more normally distributed than herbspp, though not by much. There is definitely still a little bit of clustering on the left half of the dsitribution, though fewer high extreme values.

soil %>%
    group_by(site) %>%
    summarize(veght = first(veght)) %>%
    ggplot(., aes(x = veght)) + geom_dotplot()
# The dotplot shows us that vegetation height actually looks pretty uniformly distributed, which is different from the previous two variables.
```

```{r}
# Are any of these variables correlated with each other?
soil %>%
    group_by(site) %>%
    summarize(herbspp = first(herbspp), numtreeshrub = first(numtreeshrub)) %>% 
    {cor(.$herbspp, .$numtreeshrub)} # R = 0.08

soil %>%
    group_by(site) %>%
    summarize(herbspp = first(herbspp), veght = first(veght)) %>% 
    {cor(.$herbspp, .$veght)} # R = 0.46

soil %>%
    group_by(site) %>%
    summarize(numtreeshrub = first(numtreeshrub), veght = first(veght)) %>% 
    {cor(.$numtreeshrub, .$veght)} # R = 0.27

# number of plant species and vegetation height seem to be the most correlated among these 3 variables, though it is not necessarily a strong relationship.
```

# How are these garden characteristics related to soil health?

```{r}

    group_by(site) %>%
    summarize(herbspp = first(herbspp),

    .groups = "drop") %>%

```

# Log Transforming Data 
Going to log transform variables of interest to see if the spread of variables become less skewed. This would mean using a linear model with a Normal distribution is more plausible. If data still looks really skewed, we can use a different distribution family in the models. 

Variables to log-transform
Model 1
* percent of urban land cover vs. total aps count 
* percent of urban land cover vs. n class count
* herbspp vs. aps count by garden AND n class count
* numtreeshrub vs. aps count by garden AND n class count

```{r}
# log transform URBAN250M variable
soil %>%
    group_by(site) %>%
    summarize(urban250m = first(urban250m)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = log10(urban250m))) + 
    geom_histogram()
# Doesn't look Normally distributed, probably needs a different family. skewed left

# log transform HERBSPP variable
soil %>%
    group_by(site) %>%
    summarize(herbspp = first(herbspp)) %>%
    head(., 15) %>%
    ggplot(., aes(x = log10(herbspp))) + geom_histogram()
# density curve looks skewed to the right, but a bit more normal

# log transform NUMTREESHRUB variable
soil %>%
    group_by(site) %>%
    summarize(numtreeshrub = first(numtreeshrub)) %>%
    head(., 15) %>%
    ggplot(., aes(x = log10(numtreeshrub))) + geom_histogram()
# This one looks more normally distributed. Might be best to use this garden characteristic in a linear model
```

Model 2
* NH4 vs. total aps count AND n class
* NO3 vs. total aps count AND n class
* CBH vs. total aps count AND n class


```{r}
# log transforming NH4
soil %>%
    group_by(site) %>%
    summarize(meanNH4 = mean(nh4_ug_g, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = log10(meanNH4))) + geom_density()
# right skewed

# log transforming NO3
soil %>%
    group_by(site) %>%
    summarize(meanNO3 = mean(no3_ug_g, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = log10(meanNO3))) + geom_density()
# right skewed but a bit more normal

# log transforming CBH
soil %>%
    group_by(site) %>%
    summarize(meanCBH = mean(cbh_mmol_g_h, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = log10(meanCBH))) + geom_density()
# pretty normally distributed 
```


# Modeling Soil Health Indicators Effect on Arthropod Abundance and Richness
```{r}
# Create a mixed model looking at the effects of soil health indicators (NH4, NO3, CBH) on arthropod count (abundance). Scaling predictors because CBH has different units

soil_arthct_model <- glmer(total ~ scale(nh4_ug_g) + scale(no3_ug_g) + scale(cbh_mmol_g_h) + (1 | site), data = soil, family = poisson(link = "log"))

summary(soil_arthct_model) # model doesn't suggest that any of these are significant for aps count based on the dataset

# model that includes microhabitat as an interaction term
soil_arthct_mh_interaction <- glmer(total ~ microhabitat * (scale(nh4_ug_g) + scale(no3_ug_g) + scale(cbh_mmol_g_h)) + (1 | site), data = soil, family = poisson(link = "log"))

summary(soil_arthct_mh_interaction)
# Main effect of Microhabitat Path
# possible main effect of CBH?
# interaction effect between microhabitat and soil health indicators on arthopod count
```

```{r}
# Create a mixed model looking at the effects of soil health indicators (NH4, NO3, CBH) on arthropod class count (richness). Site is held at random effect. scaling predictors to standardize
soil_richness_model <- glmer(n_class ~ scale(nh4_ug_g) + scale(no3_ug_g) + scale(cbh_mmol_g_h) + (1 | site), data = soil, family = poisson(link = "log"))

summary(soil_richness_model)
# nothing significant

soil_richness_mh_interaction <- glmer(n_class ~ microhabitat * (scale(nh4_ug_g) + scale(no3_ug_g) + scale(cbh_mmol_g_h)) + (1 | site), data = soil, family = poisson(link = "log"))

summary(soil_richness_mh_interaction)
# nothing significant either here, nothing to suggest soil health indicators or microhabitat have a significant effect on arthropod richness
```

# Modeling Garden Characteristics Effect on Arthropod Abundance and Richness

```{r}
## Mixed model looking at the effects of urban land cover, # of plant species, and # of plant individuals on arthropod count (abundance). Site and microhabitat are held at random effect

garden_abundance_model <- glmer(total ~ scale(urban250m) + scale(herbspp) + scale(numtreeshrub) + (1 | site) + (1 | microhabitat), data = soil, family = poisson(link = "log"))

summary(garden_abundance_model)
# herbspp is potentially significant, but evidence is not strong enough 

# is microhabitat a significant interaction? site is still held random. Scale the predictors because urban250m has different units. 
garden_ab_mhint_model <- glmer(total ~ microhabitat * (scale(urban250m) + scale(herbspp) + scale(numtreeshrub)) + (1 | site), data = soil, family = poisson(link = "log"))

summary(garden_ab_mhint_model)
# microhabitat might have an interaction effect on the relationships between urban cover & count, and between herbspp & count. it also has an independent effect like we saw earlier

# is vegetation height a significant interaction? it had some correlation with herbspp
garden_ab_ht_model <- glmer(total ~ scale(veght) * (scale(urban250m) + scale(herbspp) + scale(numtreeshrub)) + (1 | site), data = soil, family = poisson(link = "log"))
summary(garden_ab_ht_model)
# seems to be no significant interaction, very slight significance in interaction with numtreeshrub
```

```{r}
## Mixed model looking at the effects of urban land cover, # of plant species, and # of plant individuals on arthropod class count (richness). Site and microhabitat are held at random effect

garden_richness_model <- glmer(n_class ~ scale(urban250m) + scale(herbspp) + scale(numtreeshrub) + (1 | site) + (1 | microhabitat), data = soil, family = poisson(link = "log"))

summary(garden_richness_model)
# no evidence for significance

# is microhabitat a significant interaction? site is still held random. Scale the predictors because urban250m has different units. 
garden_rich_mhint_model <- glmer(n_class ~ microhabitat * (scale(urban250m) + scale(herbspp) + scale(numtreeshrub)) + (1 | site), data = soil, family = poisson(link = "log"))

summary(garden_rich_mhint_model)
# no evidence for significance

# is vegetation height a significant interaction? it had some correlation with herbspp
garden_rich_ht_model <- glmer(n_class ~ scale(veght) * (scale(urban250m) + scale(herbspp) + scale(numtreeshrub)) + (1 | site), data = soil, family = poisson(link = "log"))
summary(garden_rich_ht_model)
# only evidence for an interaction between veg height and numtreeshrub like in the model with abundance
```

# Checking Residual Plots for Significant Models
significant models to check plots for:
- soil_arthct_mh_interaction
- garden_ab_mhint_model


```{r}
# Running diagnostic plots for soil_arthct_mh_interaction model
library(DHARMa) # package allows us to simulate residuals using count data which we can't use with the regular diagnostic plots
simulateResiduals(fittedModel = soil_arthct_mh_interaction, plot = TRUE)
# Q-Q plot shows that deviation is significant, so this raises concerns about the fit of this data for this model
```

```{r}
# Running diagnostic plots for soil_arthct_mh_interaction model
simulateResiduals(fittedModel = garden_ab_mhint_model, plot = TRUE)
# deviation really significant
```
